The chemistry final was on Friday, and on Tuesday night Nora's notebook was gone.

She had looked in her backpack three times, and then she emptied it onto the kitchen table: two pencils, a calculator, a granola bar pressed flat as a coin. Her brother Theo, who was twelve, watched from the doorway while she went through the pockets a fourth time.

"Where did you have it last?" he asked.

"If I knew that, it wouldn't be lost."

It was a green notebook with a torn corner, and in it were four months of class notes, every lab, and the practice equations Ms. Ferrell had put on the board since January. Nora had planned to spend Wednesday and Thursday reading it from the first page to the last.

Their mother searched the living room. Theo checked under the couch cushions and behind the radiator, and then he went upstairs. When he came back down he was carrying the chemistry textbook, a stack of printer paper, and a pen.

"You could just write it again," he said.

Nora told him that was the silliest idea she had heard all week. Then, because there was nothing else to do, she sat down and tried.

It went slowly at first. She remembered that there had been a lab with copper wire and silver nitrate, but she had to work out from the textbook what it had shown. Theo read her the questions at the end of each chapter, and when she got one wrong he made her explain it until she got it right. Then, ten minutes later, without warning, in the middle of something else, he asked it again.

By Wednesday night she had eleven pages. They were messier than the old notes, and shorter, and every line was in her own words, because there were no other words to copy from.

On Thursday evening Theo came in from the driveway holding the green notebook. It had slid under the passenger seat of their mother's car, where Nora had done her homework on the ride home from school on Monday.

He held it out. Nora looked at it for a moment. Then she took it, set it on the shelf above her desk beside the dictionary, and went back to the page she was working on.

"Aren't you going to look at it?" he asked.

"Ask me the one about limiting reactants again," she said.

On Friday the last question on the exam was a limiting-reactant problem. Nora had written that page out three times. She worked it in four lines, checked it once, and turned the paper over.

item.passage:
Forty of us live above the lobby,
and in three years nobody has worked out
where to put their eyes in here.
We read the numbers as though they might change their minds.

The car is a closet
someone decided to send up into the sky.
It hums the one note it knows
and lifts us, politely, a floor at a time.

Mrs. Ocampo from nine carries her cat
in a basket with a little window,
and the cat regards each of us in turn
the way a judge regards a jury that has taken too long.

The kid from six practices trumpet
on the handrail, three silent valves,
and the man in the gray suit studies the ceiling
as if the music were coming from there.

We say Evening. We say Cold out.
We say Which floor? and press it for each other,
reaching across the little square room
like strangers passing salt down a crowded table.

Once, between four and five, it stopped.
The light stayed on. The hum went away.
For eleven minutes we were a village:
Mrs. Ocampo let the cat out of its basket,
the kid hummed the trumpet part out loud,
and the man in the gray suit told us his name was Paul.

Then the hum came back, the floor shivered,
and we all found the numbers again
as if we had been caught at something.
Paul got off at seven without a word.

I see him most evenings now.
He nods at the numbers. I nod at the numbers.
Somewhere between the lobby and seven
the cat in its basket looks from one of us to the other,
and knows.

The summer I was twelve, my aunt Delia decided I was old enough to drive the tractor. She told me this at breakfast, between a spoonful of oatmeal and a sip of coffee, as if she were telling me it might rain.

The tractor was a red Farmall older than my mother, with a seat like a metal pan and a steering wheel as wide as a bicycle tire. Its clutch took both of my feet and most of my weight. The first morning, I stalled it eleven times in the yard between the barn and the pump. Each time, Delia climbed up on the step, reached past me, and started it again. She offered no advice. She only said, "Again."

I had imagined driving fast down the lane with the dust behind me. What she had in mind was the hay. Every July her neighbors came to help bring in the bales from the long field, and someone had to drive the tractor while the others walked beside the wagon and threw the bales up. That year, she said, the someone would be me.

"How fast?" I asked.

"Slower than you think," she said. "Slow enough that Mr. Pruitt can keep up, and he is seventy-four."

For a week I practiced in the empty field. Delia walked beside the tractor and set a coffee can on the hood, and if the can slid off, I had gone too fast or turned too sharply. It slid off often. By Friday it rode the whole length of the field and back, rattling but upright.

On the day of the haying, I drove the long field at the pace of a man walking. Behind me the wagon filled. I could hear the bales land, and the neighbors talking, and once Mr. Pruitt laughing at something I missed. Nobody looked at me. I kept the wheel steady and the can on the hood, and somewhere around the third row I understood that this was the point: a driver who went unnoticed was a driver who had done the job.

When the last wagon was in the barn, Delia handed me a glass of lemonade and said that the rows had been straight. That was all she said. It was the best review I have ever received, and I have received a few since then.

I still drive too fast, most places. But when I have to do something that other people are counting on, I think of the coffee can riding on the red hood, and I slow down.

For most of its history, the town of Harlan Mills taught its children to swim in the old quarry at the edge of town, or did not teach them at all. The quarry was deep, cold, and steep-sided, and in the summers between 1915 and 1922 three boys drowned there. Each time, the town council talked about fencing it, and each time the fence was put off.

In the spring of 1923 a pharmacist named Clara Voss came before the council with a different idea. A fence, she said, would keep children out of one hole in the ground and leave them as helpless as before in every river and pond in the county. What the town needed was a place where children could learn to swim safely, and that meant a public pool.

The council was slow to agree. The cost was estimated at eleven thousand dollars, more than the town spent on its roads in a year. One member asked why the town should pay for water when the river was free. Another predicted that the pool would sit empty after the first hot week.

Voss did not argue the point. Instead she asked for the use of the high school gymnasium on Saturday mornings and gave the first lessons herself, on dry land, to anyone who came. Children lay on benches and practiced the strokes in the air while she counted. Forty came the first week. By June there were more than two hundred, and their parents had begun to ask where, exactly, the children were supposed to use what they had learned.

The council approved the pool that August, paying for half of it from the town treasury and half from a subscription that Voss's pupils collected door to door, a dime or a quarter at a time. The Harlan Mills Municipal Pool opened in July 1924, with a lifeguard's chair at one end and a painted line marking the shallow water.

The member who had predicted an empty pool lived long enough to see it crowded on summer afternoons for thirty years. In that time, the town's records show, no child drowned in the quarry. The fence that had been debated for a decade was finally built in 1931, but by then, as one councilman remarked, it was mostly keeping out children who had somewhere better to swim.

Watch a row of ducks dozing on a riverbank and you may notice something odd. The duck at the end of the row often has one eye open, and it is usually the eye facing away from the others, out toward the open bank. The duck is asleep, or at least half of it is.

Many birds can do something human beings cannot: they can rest one side of the brain while the other side stays alert. Scientists call this unihemispheric sleep, which simply means sleep in one half of the brain. Recordings of the brain's electrical activity show the sleeping half producing the slow, large waves typical of deep sleep, while the waking half looks much as it does during the day. The open eye is wired to the waking half, so the bird keeps watch with one eye while the rest of it sleeps.

The duck study that showed this most clearly was simple. Researchers filmed mallards sleeping in a row and recorded which eye each kept open. Birds in the middle of the row, flanked by neighbors, slept with both eyes closed more often. Birds at the ends kept open the eye facing outward, toward the side where a predator might come from. When an end bird turned around to face the other way, it often switched eyes as well. The birds seemed able to adjust how much of the brain they put to sleep according to the danger around them.

Half-brain sleep may also solve a harder problem. Frigatebirds, large seabirds of warm oceans, can stay in the air for days or even weeks, and a frigatebird, whose feathers are poorly waterproofed, cannot safely rest on the sea. For years scientists wondered whether such birds slept at all during those flights. In one study, researchers fitted frigatebirds with small devices that recorded brain activity during flights lasting several days. The birds did sleep in the air, but in short bursts of a few seconds, often with one half of the brain at a time, and for a total of less than an hour a day. On land, the same birds slept for more than twelve hours a day.

That last number may be the strangest of all. It suggests that frigatebirds can get by on very little sleep when they must, yet sleep a great deal when they can. How they manage the shortage, and what it costs them, is still unknown. The ducks on the riverbank keep their secrets too: half of each one is sleeping, and the other half is watching us watch them.

original_item.passage:
Watch a row of ducks dozing on a riverbank and you may notice something odd. The duck at the end of the row often has one eye open, and it is usually the eye facing away from the others, out toward the open bank. The duck is asleep, or at least half of it is.

Many birds can do something human beings cannot: they can rest one side of the brain while the other side stays alert. Scientists call this unihemispheric sleep, which simply means sleep in one half of the brain. Recordings of the brain's electrical activity show the sleeping half producing the slow, large waves typical of deep sleep, while the waking half looks much as it does during the day. The open eye is wired to the waking half, so the bird keeps watch with one eye while the rest of it sleeps.

The duck study that showed this most clearly was simple. Researchers filmed mallards sleeping in a row and recorded which eye each kept open. Birds in the middle of the row, flanked by neighbors, slept with both eyes closed more often. Birds at the ends kept open the eye facing outward, toward the side where a predator might come from. When an end bird turned around to face the other way, it often switched eyes as well. The birds seemed able to adjust how much of the brain they put to sleep according to the danger around them.

Half-brain sleep may also solve a harder problem. Frigatebirds, large seabirds of warm oceans, can stay in the air for days or even weeks, and a frigatebird, whose feathers are poorly waterproofed, cannot safely rest on the sea. For years scientists wondered whether such birds slept at all during those flights. In one study, researchers fitted frigatebirds with small devices that recorded brain activity during flights lasting several days. The birds did sleep in the air, but in short bursts of a few seconds, often with one half of the brain at a time, and for a total of less than an hour a day. On land, the same birds slept for more than twelve hours a day.

That last number may be the strangest of all. It suggests that frigatebirds can get by on very little sleep when they must, yet sleep a great deal when they can. How they manage the shortage, and what it costs them, is still unknown. The ducks on the riverbank keep their secrets too: half of each one is sleeping, and the other half is watching us watch them.
